title: The Hikam
hookLine: the Egyptian Shadhili master's short sayings, studied for seven centuries
tomorrow: one bad grade, and all your hope is gone. what does that reveal?

lines: A BOOK WITH A SOFT SPINE.
READ ONE A DAY. NOT MORE.
cards: Some people keep a folder of screenshots: one-line quotes saved at midnight, meant to be read again someday. Here is the older version.
A grandmother takes a small book from her drawer, the spine soft from handling, and presses it into her granddaughter's hands. Read one a day, she says. Not more.
It's the Hikam of Ibn Ata'illah, an Egyptian teacher of the Shadhili Sufi path. Inside: short sayings, a line or two each, meant to be chewed slowly.

teach.b: Hikam means wisdoms, plural: many small ones instead of one big argument. Here's one, paraphrased.

Your striving after what's already guaranteed to you, while you fall short in what's asked of you, is a sign your inner sight has blurred. What's guaranteed? Your provision, what God has promised to give.

What's asked? Your part: prayer, honesty, kindness, the work in front of you. The aphorism catches a very human swap: we sweat over the outcome, which isn't ours to hold, and skimp on the part that is.

So the question for today: what do I do with worry about what I'll be given? This book answers: give your full effort to what's asked, and loosen your grip on what's promised. A neighbor tradition says something close.
In Matthew's Gospel, Jesus tells a worried crowd: "But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you."
Shared ground: worry about provision shouldn't crowd out what God asks first. And an honest difference. Christians hold Matthew's words as scripture, from Jesus himself.
The Hikam isn't scripture for Muslims; it's a teacher's book, read beside the Qur'an, and its language is its own: provision guaranteed, inner sight blurred.
Two voices, two books. Neither has to become the other to be heard.

how: Ibn Ata'illah's Hikam is taught in Sufi circles and study groups one saying at a time, with a teacher explaining each; some Muslims keep a copy by the bed and read a single aphorism a day.

games.q: Jordan reads you Matthew 6:33 off his grandma's fridge and asks if the Hikam says the same thing. what's the fairest answer?
o: close neighbors on worry and provision, but one is scripture and one a teacher's book.
yes, exactly the same; every religion is really saying one thing.
no, they're opposites; one is about God and the other about money.
games.why: both say worry about provision shouldn't crowd out what God asks first. Christians hold Matthew as scripture; the Hikam is a Muslim teacher's book, with its own language.

practice: Say today's aphorism out loud, slowly, once: your striving for what's guaranteed, and your falling short in what's asked, is a sign your sight has blurred. For the sit, let one word from it stay with you, and let the rest go quiet.
